chapters.title: The Word of Blessing
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 1

1The word of blessing of Enoch, with which he blessed the chosen and the righteous, who will be there on the day of distress, when all the evil and the wicked are removed.

2And Enoch answered and said — a righteous man, whose eyes were opened by God, and he saw:

3Concerning the chosen I speak, and concerning them I took up my parable — the Great Holy One will come out from His dwelling,

4and the God of the age will tread upon Mount Sinai, and appear in the strength of His power from heaven.

5And they will fear. And the Watchers will believe, and they will sing hidden things in all the ends of the earth, and all the ends of the earth will shake.

6And the high mountains will be shaken and will fall and be broken apart, and the high hills will be brought low, and they will melt like honeycomb before the flame.

7And the earth will be split with a great chasm, and everything on the earth will be destroyed, and there will be judgment on all.

8And with the righteous He will make peace, and over the chosen there will be protection and peace, and He will help them.

9And here — He came with ten thousands of holy ones, to carry out judgment on them, and to destroy the wicked, and to bring a charge against all flesh for everything that sinners and the wicked have done and committed against Him.

Notes

  • On this book and how it is rendered — 1 Enoch does not survive whole in the language it was written in. The complete text exists only in Ge'ez (classical Ethiopic), a translation of a translation. Behind it stand fragments of Greek, and behind those, fragments of the Aramaic original found at Qumran among the Dead Sea Scrolls. This rendering follows the fullest witness at each point and the notes say which one that is. Where a witness is missing a line the others have, that is reported rather than smoothed over.

  • v1 "when all the evil and the wicked are removed" — the Ge'ez says the evil and the wicked. The Greek says all the enemies — a political word, not a moral one. The Greek also closes the verse with four words the Ge'ez does not have at all: and the righteous will be saved.

  • v1 "the chosen and the righteous" — the Ge'ez joins them with and, making two groups. The Greek has no and: chosen righteous, one group described twice. The whole book turns on who the chosen are, and the two witnesses disagree in the opening sentence about whether that is one category or two.

  • v3–4 "the Great Holy One will come out from His dwelling" — this half-line is not in the Ge'ez, which runs straight from the Holy One who goes forth into and the God of the age. It is in the Aramaic: the Gr[eat] Holy One will go forth from — and in the Greek. The Qumran fragment is the oldest witness on the page and it has a line the complete Ethiopic text lost.

  • v4 "in the strength of His power" — again from the Aramaic: he will appear in the [might] of [his] streng[th]. The Ge'ez instead says He appears in His camp — an army rather than a display of force. The Greek is broken off at exactly this point and cannot settle it.

  • v5 "the Watchers" — the entire Ge'ez verse is two words: and they will fear. The Greek has all will be afraid, and the Watchers will believe, and they will sing hidden things in all the ends of the earth. The Aramaic independently confirms the ending: [al]l the end[s of the earth will tremble]. The Watchers — egrēgoroi in Greek, the sleepless ones — are the subject of chapters 6 through 16 and the reason the book exists. The complete Ethiopic text drops them from their first appearance.

  • v6 "melt like honeycomb before the flame" — the image is in the Ge'ez only; the Greek breaks off before it. The Greek gives the mountains three verbs where the Ge'ez gives one — shaken, fall, dissolved. The single Ge'ez verb is built on a root used for being startled or terrified, so it may carry more than physical shaking, but it is regularly used of things trembling and the sense here cannot be pinned down from this verse alone.

  • v7 "the earth will be split with a great chasm" — the Ge'ez has two words here: and it will sink. The Greek has the whole verse: the earth splits, everything on it perishes, judgment comes on all. Two witnesses, two different ends of the world — one drowns, one cracks open.

  • v8 "with the righteous He will make peace" — the Greek says with; the Ge'ez says upon. And where the Ge'ez says righteous twice, the Greek distinguishes: peace with the righteous, protection and peace upon the chosen. If those are two groups, this verse promises them different things.

  • v9 "And here — He came" — this is the verse the New Testament quotes. Jude 14–15 attributes it to Enoch, the seventh from Adam, and quotes it closely: Behold, the Lord came with his holy myriads, to execute judgment against all and to convict all the ungodly. Jude's last two words are sinners, ungodly — the same pair in the same order that ends this verse in the Ge'ez. Jude uses a past tense, came, as does the surviving Latin scrap (Ecce venit), while the Greek witness here has the present, he comes. The Ge'ez verb is the perfect form — grammatically past — but Semitic prophecy regularly states a future event in the perfect, as something already accomplished, so the form does not settle the tense. What can be said is that a New Testament letter quotes this book as prophecy, and quotes it closely.

chapters.title: Observe All the Works in Heaven
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 2

1Observe all the works in heaven, how they do not change their paths — and the lights in heaven, how each one rises and sets, each ordered in its appointed time, and they appear at their festivals, and they do not overstep their own order.

2Look at the earth, and think carefully about the works that are done on it, from first to last: how none of God's works changes, and all of them appear to you.

3Look at the signs of summer and of winter, how the whole earth is filled with water, and the clouds pour out rain over it.

Notes

  • v1 "Observe" — the first word of a sequence that runs from here to the end of chapter 5. Four times the reader is told to look at something in nature — the stars, the earth, the trees, the seasons — and each time the point is the same: they keep to their orders. The argument the book is building is that people do not.

  • v1 "each ordered in its appointed time, and they appear at their festivals" — the Ge'ez stops halfway through this verse; the Greek carries it to the end. This is not decorative. The whole of 1 Enoch 72–82 is a solar calendar argued against the lunar one, and they appear at their festivals is the opening move: the feast days are set by the lights, and the lights do not drift.

  • v2 "Look at the earth" — the Ge'ez has two words, Look at, and then nothing. The Greek continues: and consider the works that are in it. The Aramaic from Qumran has it too, and adds a word the others lack — Co[ntemplate] the earth and o[bse]rve its works — the earth's own works, not God's works on the earth.

  • v3 "the signs of summer and of winter" — the word signs is in the Aramaic only. The Ge'ez and Greek both say simply summer and winter; the Aramaic says the signs of summer and the signs of winter. A sign is something meant to be read. The oldest witness makes the seasons a text, and the two later ones make them weather.

  • v3 "the clouds pour out rain" — the Aramaic is the longest witness here, the only one of the three that names the clouds pouring. The Greek breaks off mid-verse and the Ge'ez gives a list — water, and cloud and dew and rain — without a verb.

speech.text: 1 Enoch 2

Observe all the works in heaven, how they do not change their paths — and the lights in heaven, how each one rises and sets, each ordered in its appointed time, and they appear at their festivals, and they do not overstep their own order.
Look at the earth, and think carefully about the works that are done on it, from first to last: how none of God's works changes, and all of them appear to you.
Look at the signs of summer and of winter, how the whole earth is filled with water, and the clouds pour out rain over it.

chapters.title: The Trees That Do Not Shed
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 3

1Observe and see how all the trees look withered, and all their leaves are stripped off — except fourteen trees, which do not shed, but keep the old leaves for two or three years until the new ones come.

Notes

  • v1 "fourteen trees" — the number is in the Ge'ez alone. The Greek here is a torn line that reads only observe and see all the trees, and the Aramaic says all the tr[ees], all of them, appear withered — with no exception made for fourteen of them. The oldest witness may simply be broken at the point where the exception stood, or the exception may be later. The count is not checkable from the earliest text.

  • v1 "keep the old leaves for two or three years" — this clause is not in the Ge'ez, which ends at do not shed their leaves. It is in the Aramaic: [their] lea[ves] remain [... until] two or three [years pass]. A detail about evergreens that the complete Ethiopic text lost and a Dead Sea fragment kept.

  • On the shortest chapter — one verse, and all three witnesses disagree about its content. It is a fair sample of what reading this book is like.

speech.text: 1 Enoch 3

Observe and see how all the trees look withered, and all their leaves are stripped off — except fourteen trees, which do not shed, but keep the old leaves for two or three years until the new ones come.

chapters.title: The Heat of Summer
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 4

1And again observe the days of summer, how the sun is above the earth and right over against it. And you look for shade and shelter from the heat of the sun, and the earth burns with scorching heat, and you cannot walk on the ground or on the rock because of its heat.

Notes

  • v1 — there is no Greek for this chapter. The witnesses are the Ge'ez and a torn Aramaic fragment, and they agree closely: the searching for shade, the inability to walk on ground or rock, the heat. Where two witnesses this far apart in age and language line up phrase by phrase, the wording behind both is likely close to original.

  • v1 "observe the days of summer" — the Aramaic again has the signs of summer, as it did in 2:3, where the Ge'ez has days. The same difference twice in two chapters is a pattern, not a slip: one tradition is reading the seasons as signs to be interpreted, the other as periods of time.

  • v1 "you cannot walk on the ground or on the rock" — the Aramaic reads the du[st] and on its rocks. Dust, not ground. It is the word from Genesis 2:7, the stuff the first man was made of, and the sun makes it untouchable.

speech.text: 1 Enoch 4

And again observe the days of summer, how the sun is above the earth and right over against it. And you look for shade and shelter from the heat of the sun, and the earth burns with scorching heat, and you cannot walk on the ground or on the rock because of its heat.

chapters.title: But You Have Not Held Fast
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 5

1Observe how the trees cover themselves with green leaves, and how all their fruit is for honor and glory. Think carefully about all His works, and understand that the living God made them so, and that He lives for all the ages.

2And all His works stand before Him, going on from year to year in the same way, and all His works carry out their tasks for Him and do not change — everything happens just as it was commanded.

3And see how the sea and the rivers do the same, and do not change their works from His word.

4But you have not held fast, and you have not done according to His commandments. You have turned away, and you have spoken great and hard words with your unclean mouth against His greatness. You have spoken against Him in your lies, you hard-hearted — there is no peace for you.

5And because of this you will curse your days, and the years of your life will be destroyed.

6Then your names will become an everlasting curse to all the righteous, and by you all who curse will curse, and all the sinners and the wicked will swear by you.

7And for the chosen there will be light and favor and peace, and they will inherit the earth. But for you, the wicked, there will be a curse.

8Then light and favor will be given to the chosen, and they will inherit the earth. Then wisdom will be given to all the chosen, and they will all live, and they will never sin again — not through unfaithfulness and not through pride. In the enlightened man there will be light, and in the understanding man, insight, and they will not go wrong.

9And they will not sin all the days of their life, and they will not die in burning anger, but they will complete the number of the days of their life. And their life will grow in peace, and the years of their joy will be multiplied in gladness and in everlasting peace, through all the days of their life.

Notes

  • v1 "for honor and glory" — the phrase is in the Greek and, broken, in the Aramaic (for maj]estic splen[dor). It is not in the Ge'ez, which says only that the trees bear fruit. The point of the whole nature sequence turns on it: the fruit is not for eating, it is for honor. Obedience is being described as a kind of beauty.

  • v2 "everything happens just as it was commanded" — the Ge'ez breaks off at but just as, mid-sentence. The Greek finishes it, and the Aramaic independently has all of them perform his word. Where the Ge'ez runs out of sentence, two older witnesses agree on how it ended.

  • v4 "you have spoken great and hard words with your unclean mouth" — the Ge'ez has one word for this verse: But you. Everything else here comes from the Greek, and the Aramaic confirms it almost phrase for phrase: But you have changed your works [... and have spo]ken against him great and harsh words with the mouth of your impurity; [... hearts,] there will be no peace for you. This is the sharpest gap in the chapter. The complete Ethiopic text loses the entire charge — and the charge is the reason for everything that follows.

  • v4 "there is no peace for you" — a refrain in this book, and it lands on the accused rather than on their circumstances. Nothing is said about what will happen to them. It is said about what they are.

  • v5 "the years of your life will be destroyed" — the Ge'ez has the years of your life; the Aramaic has only Then your days; the Greek breaks off at Therefore your days you. All three witnesses are damaged in the same verse.

  • v6 "all the sinners and the wicked will swear by you" — a name used in an oath is a name people trust. The curse is that these names stay in use — as the standard of what a wrecked life looks like.

  • v8 "wisdom will be given to all the chosen" — the Ge'ez has two words here, And then, and stops. The whole of this verse is Greek: wisdom, life, the end of sin, light in the enlightened man, insight in the understanding one. It is the most hopeful sentence in the first five chapters of the book, and the complete Ethiopic text does not have it.

  • v9 "they will complete the number of the days of their life" — the promise is not immortality. It is that the count runs out on time. Against chapter 6, where two hundred beings come down and ruin exactly this, it is the whole argument of the book stated in advance.

speech.text: 1 Enoch 5

And all His works stand before Him, going on from year to year in the same way, and all His works carry out their tasks for Him and do not change — everything happens just as it was commanded.
And see how the sea and the rivers do the same, and do not change their works from His word.

But you have not held fast, and you have not done according to His commandments. You have turned away, and you have spoken great and hard words with your unclean mouth against His greatness. You have spoken against Him in your lies, you hard-hearted — there is no peace for you.
And because of this you will curse your days, and the years of your life will be destroyed.
Then your names will become an everlasting curse to all the righteous, and by you all who curse will curse, and all the sinners and the wicked will swear by you.

chapters.title: In the Days of Jared
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 6

1And it came to pass, when the sons of men had multiplied in those days, that beautiful daughters were born to them.

2And the angels, the sons of heaven, saw them and desired them, and said to one another, "Come, let us choose wives for ourselves from the sons of men, and let us father children for ourselves."

3And Semyaza, who was their leader, said to them, "I am afraid you will not want this deed done, and I alone will pay the penalty for this great sin."

4And they all answered him and said, "Let us all swear an oath, and bind ourselves to one another under a curse, that we will not turn back from this plan, but will carry this plan out in fact."

5Then they all swore together, and all bound themselves to one another under a curse upon it.

6And they were two hundred in all, and they came down in the days of Jared onto the summit of Mount Hermon.

7And these are the names of their chiefs: Semyaza, who was their leader, Urakibarameel, Akibeel, Tamiel, Ramuel, Danel, Ezeqeel, Saraquyal, Asael, Armaros, Batarael, Ananel, Zaqeel, Samsapeel, Satarel, Turel, Yomyael, Arazyal.

8These are their chiefs — the chiefs of the tens.

Notes

  • v1 "when the sons of men had multiplied... beautiful daughters were born to them" — this is Genesis 6:1 almost word for word: And it came to pass, when men began to multiply on the face of the ground, and daughters were born to them. Genesis then gives the episode four verses and moves on to the flood. 1 Enoch gives it ten chapters. Whichever direction the borrowing ran, the two books are telling the same story, and only one of them explains it.

  • v2 "the angels, the sons of heaven" — Genesis 6:2 calls them bene ha-Elohim, the sons of God, and says nothing more about who they are. This book calls them angels in its second sentence on the subject and never treats the question as open.

  • v3 "I alone will pay the penalty" — the leader's objection is not that the plan is wrong. It is that he will be left holding it. The oath in the next verse is his solution: make everyone equally guilty. The book's account of how a group does something none of them would do alone is four verses long and has not dated.

  • v6 "in the days of Jared" — the Ge'ez does not say this. It says they came down on Ardis, a place name that appears nowhere else. The Greek says in the days of Jared upon the summit of Mount Hermoniem, and the Aramaic from Qumran confirms it: in the days of Jared up[on.... So the older witnesses date the descent and the Ethiopic names a mountain instead.

  • v6 "Jared" — in Genesis 5:18, Jared is Enoch's father. The name in Hebrew is Yered, from the verb yarad, to come down. The Watchers come down in the days of Descent. The Aramaic has the same consonants for the name and the act, and this is one of the few wordplays in the book that can be checked in the original language rather than through a translation.

  • v6 "Mount Hermon" — the name is in the Greek (Hermoniem); the Aramaic fragment breaks off just before it. In Hebrew, cherem is the word for something placed under a ban or a binding curse — which is exactly what the two hundred have just done to each other in vv4–5. No surviving witness says the two words are connected. The mountain and the oath simply carry the same sound, and the text puts them one verse apart.

  • v7 "Urakibarameel" — the list has eighteen names. The next verse says these are the chiefs of the tens, and two hundred split into tens needs twenty chiefs. The list does not reach the number the text itself gives. This name in particular looks like two run together, which would make nineteen.

  • v8 "the chiefs of the tens" — the Ge'ez verse is two words: These are. The Greek has These are the chiefs of their tens, and the Aramaic has the most of all three: These are the chiefs, and the chief[s] of the ten[s] — two ranks, not one. The complete Ethiopic text stops before the only line that tells you how the two hundred were organized.
